name: Siberian ginseng (Eleutherococcus senticosus)
short: Adverse-event reports judged causal: gut, nose, vaginal bleeding with antidepressants. Case report: high digoxin level, unclear if real or a test error. Trial in 20 on digitalis: no adverse events.
text: Human safety evidence for Siberian ginseng is limited and comes mainly from adverse-event reports, a case report and a small trial. A retrospective review of 1,816 adverse-event reports in people taking antidepressants found that adaptogenic herbs were involved in 9% of events linked to combined use with other preparations, and identified 30 reports, across all the adaptogens studied, judged to have a causal relationship; those listed for Eleutherococcus senticosus were upper gastrointestinal bleeding (with duloxetine), nosebleed (with paroxetine), vaginal bleeding (with sertraline), and irritability, agitation, headache and dizziness (with agomelatine), and the abstract does not say how many reports involved this herb. A case report described a 74-year-old man on long-term digoxin whose blood digoxin level was high, with no signs of toxicity, and stayed high after digoxin was stopped, while he took Siberian ginseng; it fell when he stopped the ginseng, rose when he restarted it and fell again when he stopped once more, and the author could not tell whether a ginseng component was converted to digoxin in the body, interfered with digoxin elimination or caused a false test result. A laboratory study found that some Siberian ginseng preparations interfered with two of five digoxin blood tests, falsely raising the result with one and lowering it with another, with no interference in the other three; in animal data, mice fed ginseng showed apparent digoxin activity in serum. In contrast, in an 8-week randomised trial in 20 older adults with high blood pressure who were taking digitalis (10 given Eleutherococcus extract, 10 placebo), no adverse events were observed and there was no significant difference in blood pressure control or digitalis blood levels.
